behavior_items: The reproducer defines a non-template outer type `struct S` containing a nested named union declaration `union U { int m; };`. This makes `S::U` a valid member type, and its actual class-key is `union`.

The function template `template <typename T> void f()` contains the declaration `union T::U u;`. Syntactically, this is an elaborated-type-specifier using the class-key `union` followed by a dependent qualified-id `T::U`. The intent is to declare a local variable `u` whose type is the nested union `U` inside whatever type `T` names.

Because `T::U` is dependent, name lookup and kind resolution are deferred until template instantiation. During the initial template definition, the compiler must treat `T::U` as a dependent type name rather than immediately classify it as some specific complete type declaration from a known context.

When `main` calls `f<S>()`, substitution makes the declaration effectively become `union S::U u;`. Since `S::U` was declared as a union member type, this instantiated declaration is well-formed: the elaborated-type-specifier uses the matching class-key for the member type.

The bug report highlights the standard rule from template name resolution that dependent qualified names are resolved at instantiation, and nothing in that rule gives `union` special treatment different from `struct` or `class`. Therefore, if `struct T::U` or `class T::U` participates in dependent lookup machinery, `union T::U` should as well.

GCC instead diagnoses the declaration as `‘union’ tag used in naming ‘class T::U’`, which shows that internally it classifies the dependent member type under a generic or incorrect `class` category before actual instantiation confirms that the nested type is specifically a union.

The wording of GCC's error is significant: it does not say `T::U` is not a type, nor that `typename` is required, nor that the qualified name is invalid. It specifically objects to a mismatch between the written class-key `union` and GCC's internal view of the dependent type as `class T::U`. That points to a front-end bug in elaborated-type handling for dependent qualified names, not a semantic problem in the user code.

The reproducer is minimal because it isolates exactly one behavior: a dependent nested type referred to with the `union` class-key inside a template. The outer container `S`, the nested `U`, and the instantiation `f<S>()` are all just enough to force template-dependent qualified type resolution.

The variable declaration itself has no runtime significance; the bug is purely compile-time. The body of `f` only declares an automatic object `u` of union type, and `main` simply instantiates the template. There is no need to access `u.m` or perform union operations, because the failure happens before code generation.

The fact that clang, ICC, and MSVC accept the code indicates the program exercises standard-conforming dependent type resolution behavior that other compilers implement correctly. GCC's rejection across many versions suggests a longstanding parser or semantic-analysis defect specific to dependent elaborated-type-specifiers using `union`.

A subtle point exercised by the reproducer is that `union` here is not introducing a new declaration; it is naming an existing nested type through an elaborated type form. GCC appears to mishandle this when the named type is dependent, likely by normalizing dependent class types to `class`/`struct`-like handling while forgetting that `union` must remain a permitted class-key until instantiation determines the actual entity.

The example also demonstrates that nested unions participate in member type lookup just like nested structs or classes. The reproducer therefore checks whether GCC's template resolution path treats all class-keys uniformly for dependent qualified names, and the observed failure shows it does not.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The code defines `S::U` as a nested union and then, inside a function template, declares `u` as `union T::U`. This exercises dependent qualified type lookup through an elaborated-type-specifier with the class-key `union`. Instantiating `f<S>()` should produce `union S::U u;`, which is valid because `S::U` is in fact a union. GCC incorrectly rejects the code by treating the dependent name as if it were a generic or mismatched `class T::U`, reporting a class-key mismatch. The reproducer therefore isolates a GCC front-end bug in template name resolution/elaborated-type handling for dependent nested union types, not a problem with the program itself.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: Patterns: (1) the failure is purely in the C++ front end during parsing/semantic analysis of templates, not in code generation; (2) the trigger is an elaborated-type-specifier using the class-key `union` on a dependent qualified name `T::U`; (3) `T::U` should remain unresolved until instantiation, but GCC reports a tag-kind mismatch as if it had already classified the dependent name as `class T::U`; (4) after substitution with `T=S`, the declaration becomes `union S::U u;`, which is valid because `S::U` is actually a nested union. The common pattern therefore points to GCC prematurely or incorrectly normalizing dependent member types in elaborated-type handling, with `union` not treated uniformly with `struct`/`class` in template name resolution.
possible_causes: Bug in the dependent elaborated-type-specifier path in the C++ front end (likely around `cp_parser_elaborated_type_specifier`, `groktypename`, or `xref_tag`): `union T::U` is being sent through a generic class/struct handling path and rejected before correct dependent resolution.

Bug in dependent type construction/canonicalization (e.g. `make_typename_type` or related typename builders): GCC may be dropping the written `union` class-key and creating a placeholder internally classified as a generic `class`/record type, which later produces the false diagnostic.

Premature tag-kind validation: code that checks whether the written class-key matches the referenced type is likely running before template instantiation, instead of deferring the check until substitution resolves `T::U` to the actual nested type `S::U`.

Instantiation/resolution bug in template substitution (`tsubst` or dependent qualified lookup): after substituting `T=S`, GCC may fail to re-evaluate or update the placeholder's tag kind from the pre-instantiation generic class form to the resolved union type.

Incomplete class-key compatibility logic for dependent names: GCC likely has logic that treats dependent `struct`/`class` cases as acceptable but omits `union`, even though the standard's dependent-name resolution rules do not give `union` special exclusion.
evidence: `S::U` is explicitly declared as `union U { int m; };`, so the instantiated form `union S::U u;` is well-formed.
The only dependent part is the qualified member type `T::U`; this is exactly the kind of lookup that must be deferred until template instantiation.

gcc/cp/decl.cc.summary: We're initializing a local variable which has a cleanup GUARD. If there are any temporaries used in the initializer INIT of this variable, we need to wrap their cleanups with TRY_CATCH_EXPR (, GUARD) so that the variable will be cleaned up properly if one of them throws. Unfortunately, there's no way to express this properly in terms of nesting, as the regions for the temporaries overlap the region for the variable itself; if there are two temporaries, the variable needs to be the first thing destroyed if either of the temporary destructors throws. However, we only want to run the variable's cleanup if it actually got constructed. So we need to guard the temporary cleanups with the variable's cleanup if they are run on the normal path, but not if they are run on the exceptional path. We implement this by telling honor_protect_cleanup_actions to strip the variable cleanup from the exceptional path. Another approach could be to make the variable cleanup region enclose initialization, but depend on a flag to indicate that the variable is initialized; that's effectively what we do for arrays. But the current approach works fine for non-arrays, and has no code overhead in the usual case

gcc/cp/decl.cc.summary: Create the FUNCTION_DECL for a function definition. DECLSPECS and DECLARATOR are the parts of the declaration; they describe the function's name and the type it returns, but twisted together in a fashion that parallels the syntax of C. FLAGS is a bitwise or of SF_PRE_PARSED (indicating that the DECLARATOR is really the DECL for the function we are about to process and that DECLSPECS should be ignored), SF_INCLASS_INLINE indicating that the function is an inline defined in-class. This function creates a binding context for the function body as well as setting up the FUNCTION_DECL in current_function_decl. For C++, we must first check whether that datum makes any sense. For example, "class A local_a(1,2);" means that variable local_a is an aggregate of type A, which should have a constructor applied to it with the argument list [1, 2]. On entry, DECL_INITIAL (decl1) should be NULL_TREE or error_mark_node, or may be a BLOCK if the function has been defined previously in this translation unit. On exit, DECL_INITIAL (decl1) will be error_mark_node if the function has never been defined, or a BLOCK if the function has been defined somewhere.

reviewed_methods.signature: tree strip_typedefs (tree t, bool *remove_attributes , unsigned int flags )
reviewed_methods.summary: Builds a qualified variant of T that is either not a typedef variant (the default behavior) or not a typedef variant of a user-facing type (if FLAGS contains STF_USER_VISIBLE). If T is not a type, then this just dispatches to strip_typedefs_expr. E.g. consider the following declarations: typedef const int ConstInt; typedef ConstInt* PtrConstInt; If T is PtrConstInt, this function returns a type representing const int*. In other words, if T is a typedef, the function returns the underlying type. The cv-qualification and attributes of the type returned match the input type. They will always be compatible types. The returned type is built so that all of its subtypes recursively have their typedefs stripped as well. This is different from just returning TYPE_CANONICAL (T) Because of several reasons: If T is a type that needs structural equality its TYPE_CANONICAL (T) will be NULL. TYPE_CANONICAL (T) desn't carry type attributes and loses template parameter names. If REMOVE_ATTRIBUTES is non-null, also strip attributes that don't affect type identity, and set the referent to true if any were stripped.
